question: The label of a vitamin bottle sold in the US. Which line, in the smallest print, matters most?
answer: The asterisk. Under a 1994 US law, supplements are sold without approval and may claim to support a body function, as long as this disclaimer sits beside the claim. They may not claim to treat a disease. So a label can sound medical while saying, in law, that nobody checked.
move: Read the small print first; it says what nobody checked.
ask: Which health claim did I believe this year without noticing who, if anyone, checked it?

scene.head: Dietary supplement
scene.title: Immune support
scene.body: Supports a healthy immune system.* Clinically researched ingredients. *These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration.

phrases.plain: Claims to help a body function, no proof needed.*
phrases.why: A structure-function claim: the maker only has to notify the FDA, not show it works.

phrases.plain: Ingredients someone has studied, for something
phrases.why: Researched is not proven. It doesn't say for what, at what dose, or with what result.
The law makes the maker print this beside the claim. It is where the evidence is missing.

scene.ask: One line is the law saying nobody checked. Which?
scene.watch: Follow the asterisk. Where a claim leads to small print, the evidence stops.

reference: US Food and Drug Administration, Structure/function claims for dietary supplements under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994
